theory.intro: Two non-zero vectors are **perpendicular** exactly when their dot product is zero. So to test for a right angle, work out the dot product and check whether it comes to $0$.
facts: For non-zero vectors, $\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}=0$ if and only if $\underset{\sim}{a}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}$ are perpendicular.
A non-zero dot product means the vectors are not perpendicular. A positive dot product means the angle is acute or $0^{\circ}$; a negative dot product means the angle is obtuse or $180^{\circ}$.
In two dimensions, $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}$ is perpendicular to $\begin{pmatrix}-y\\x\end{pmatrix}$: swap the components and change one sign.
To find an unknown component, write the dot product, set it equal to zero, and solve.
Both vectors must be non-zero, since the zero vector has a zero dot product with everything and has no direction.
steps: Write the dot product of the two vectors
Set the dot product equal to zero
Solve for the unknown and reject any value making a vector zero

workedExamples.question_text:
Use the dot product to determine whether each pair of vectors is perpendicular.

(a) $\underset{\sim}{u}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=\begin{pmatrix}15\\-6\end{pmatrix}$.

(b) $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\end{pmatrix}$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a)

$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{u}\cdot\underset{\sim}{v}&=(2)(15)+(5)(-6)\\&=30-30\\&=0\end{aligned}$

Both vectors are non-zero and their dot product is zero, so they are perpendicular.

(b)

$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}&=(4)(2)+(-3)(5)\\&=8-15\\&=-7\end{aligned}$

The dot product is not zero, so these vectors are not perpendicular.

Perpendicular non-zero vectors have dot product zero.

$\begin{aligned}(3)(m)+(7)(-6)&=0\\3m-42&=0\\3m&=42\\m&=14\end{aligned}$

Neither vector is zero when $m=14$, so this value is valid.

Use vectors starting at the angle's vertex, $B$.

$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{BA}&=\begin{pmatrix}1-5\\2-4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-2\end{pmatrix}\\\overrightarrow{BC}&=\begin{pmatrix}3-5\\8-4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\4\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}&=(-4)(-2)+(-2)(4)\\&=8-8\\&=0\end{aligned}$

Both vectors are non-zero, so $\overrightarrow{BA}\perp\overrightarrow{BC}$ and $\angle ABC=90^{\circ}$.

workedExamples.question_text: Find all values of $t$ for which $\underset{\sim}{u}=\begin{pmatrix}t\\4\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=\begin{pmatrix}t+3\\-7\end{pmatrix}$ are perpendicular.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Set the dot product equal to zero.

$\begin{aligned}(t)(t+3)+(4)(-7)&=0\\t^{2}+3t-28&=0\\(t+7)(t-4)&=0\end{aligned}$

$t=-7$ or $t=4$.

The fixed components $4$ and $-7$ ensure both vectors are non-zero, so both values are valid.

workedExamples.question_text: Find all values of $k$ for which $\underset{\sim}{u}=\begin{pmatrix}k-4\\k-4\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=\begin{pmatrix}k\\2\end{pmatrix}$ are perpendicular.
workedExamples.solution_text:
First solve the zero-dot-product equation.

$\begin{aligned}(k-4)k+(k-4)(2)&=0\\(k-4)(k+2)&=0\end{aligned}$

$k=4$ or $k=-2$.

When $k=4$, $\underset{\sim}{u}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}$. The zero vector has no direction, so reject this value.

When $k=-2$, $\underset{\sim}{u}=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\-6\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Both are non-zero and their dot product is zero.

Therefore, $k=-2$ only.

development.question_text:
The vectors $\underset{\sim}{u}=5\underset{\sim}{i}+2\underset{\sim}{j}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=8\underset{\sim}{i}+t\underset{\sim}{j}$ are perpendicular.
Find the value of $t$.

The vectors $\begin{pmatrix}2\\m\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\end{pmatrix}$ are perpendicular.
Find the value of $m$.

The points $A(1,3)$, $B(5,6)$ and $C(8,2)$ are given.
Show that $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is perpendicular to $\overrightarrow{BC}$.
development.solution_text:
$\overrightarrow{AB}=(5-1,\,6-3)=\begin{pmatrix}4\\3\end{pmatrix}$
$\overrightarrow{BC}=(8-5,\,2-6)=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-4\end{pmatrix}$
$\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}$
$=(4)(3)+(3)(-4)$
$=12-12$
$=0$
The dot product is zero, so $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is perpendicular to $\overrightarrow{BC}$.

development.question_text:
The points $P(-2,4)$, $Q(4,2)$ and $R(6,8)$ are given.
Show that $\angle PQR=90^{\circ}$.
development.solution_text:
$\overrightarrow{QP}=(-2-4,\,4-2)=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\2\end{pmatrix}$
$\overrightarrow{QR}=(6-4,\,8-2)=\begin{pmatrix}2\\6\end{pmatrix}$
$\overrightarrow{QP}\cdot\overrightarrow{QR}$
$=(-6)(2)+(2)(6)$
$=-12+12$
$=0$
Both vectors start at $Q$ and their dot product is zero, so $\angle PQR=90^{\circ}$.

Find the values of $t$ for which $\underset{\sim}{a}=\begin{pmatrix}2t\\t+1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{b}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-t\end{pmatrix}$ are perpendicular.
development.solution_text:
$(2t)(3)+(t+1)(-t)=0$
$6t-t^{2}-t=0$
$5t-t^{2}=0$
$t(5-t)=0$
$t=0$ or $t=5$
Neither value makes $\underset{\sim}{a}$ or $\underset{\sim}{b}$ the zero vector, so both are valid.

mastery.question_text:
The points $A(0,1)$, $B(6,-1)$, $C(9,8)$ and $D(3,10)$ are the vertices of a quadrilateral $ABCD$.
Show that the angles at $B$ and at $D$ are both right angles.
mastery.solution_text:
$\overrightarrow{BA}=(0-6,\,1-(-1))=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\2\end{pmatrix}$
$\overrightarrow{BC}=(9-6,\,8-(-1))=\begin{pmatrix}3\\9\end{pmatrix}$
$\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=(-6)(3)+(2)(9)=-18+18=0$
$\overrightarrow{DA}=(0-3,\,1-10)=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-9\end{pmatrix}$
$\overrightarrow{DC}=(9-3,\,8-10)=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-2\end{pmatrix}$
$\overrightarrow{DA}\cdot\overrightarrow{DC}=(-3)(6)+(-9)(-2)=-18+18=0$
Both dot products are zero, so the angles at $B$ and at $D$ are right angles.

mastery.question_text: Find the values of $p$ for which $\begin{pmatrix}p+1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}p\\-6\end{pmatrix}$ are perpendicular.
Find all values of $k$ for which $\underset{\sim}{u}=\begin{pmatrix}k-2\\k-2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=\begin{pmatrix}k\\3\end{pmatrix}$ are perpendicular.
mastery.solution_text:
$(k-2)(k)+(k-2)(3)=0$
$(k-2)(k+3)=0$
$k=2$ or $k=-3$
When $k=2$, $\underset{\sim}{u}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}$, which has no direction, so it cannot be perpendicular to anything.
$k=-3$
